stem: An organization wants to restrict resource deployment to approved regions. Which governance service is a natural fit?

choices.A: Azure Policy
choices.B: Azure Pricing Calculator
choices.D: Azure Advisor

explanations.A: A policy can enforce an allowed-location rule.
explanations.B: The calculator estimates costs.
explanations.C: Service Health reports service events.
explanations.D: Advisor recommends improvements rather than applying that deployment rule.

stem: What is a policy definition?

choices.A: An automatic grant of Contributor rights
choices.B: A list of billed transactions
choices.D: A description of a rule and its effect

explanations.A: Policy does not itself grant Azure RBAC access.
explanations.B: That is usage information.
explanations.C: Definitions are governance objects.
explanations.D: The definition contains the reusable evaluation logic.

stem: A built-in policy is listed in a subscription. What is still needed to apply it to a chosen scope?

choices.A: Changing the billing currency
choices.B: Adding a Reader role definition
choices.D: A policy assignment

explanations.A: Currency does not apply a policy rule.
explanations.B: A role definition is not a policy assignment.
explanations.C: Renaming does not assign the definition.
explanations.D: An assignment connects the definition to an evaluation scope.

stem: What is an Azure Policy initiative?

choices.A: A collection of authentication factors
choices.B: A storage redundancy option
choices.D: A collection of policy definitions managed together

explanations.A: Factors belong to identity sign-in.
explanations.B: Redundancy describes data replication.
explanations.C: Images define operating-system disks.
explanations.D: Initiatives group related governance rules.

stem: A policy uses the audit effect for an unwanted configuration. What is the intended result?

choices.A: Grant every user permission to repair resources
choices.B: Record noncompliance without blocking that configuration through this effect
choices.D: Permanently freeze the subscription

explanations.A: Permissions are a separate concern.
explanations.B: Audit reports the finding rather than denying the request.
explanations.C: Audit is not deletion.
explanations.D: Audit does not impose a read-only lock.

stem: A new resource request violates an applicable deny policy. What can happen?

choices.A: The policy grants the missing permissions
choices.B: The request is rejected even if the user has resource-write permissions
choices.C: The violation is ignored for every Owner
choices.D: The resource is created only in the user's home tenant

explanations.A: Policy does not grant RBAC rights.
explanations.B: Authorization and policy evaluation both matter.
explanations.C: Ownership does not universally bypass governance rules.
explanations.D: Policy denial is not a tenant migration.

stem: What determines where a policy assignment applies?

choices.A: The assignment scope and any configured exclusions
choices.B: The resource group's location field alone
choices.D: The caller's resource role definition name

explanations.A: Scope defines the governed resource boundary.
explanations.B: Deployment location is not the complete governed hierarchy scope.
explanations.C: The rule's label does not determine assignment scope.
explanations.D: A role determines permitted actions rather than the policy assignment's target boundary.

stem: A team wants to report resources missing a required tag before enforcing it. Which effect fits the first stage?

choices.A: CanNotDelete
choices.B: Reader
choices.D: Deny

explanations.A: That is a management lock level.
explanations.B: Reader is an Azure RBAC role.
explanations.C: Audit supports assessment without that rule denying deployment.
explanations.D: Deny blocks matching noncompliant requests.

stem: A learner reads az policy definition list. What has the learner changed?

choices.A: All resources' required tags
choices.B: Every subscription's policy scope
choices.C: No policy assignment through that read command
choices.D: The selected tenant's users

explanations.A: Listing definitions does not remediate tags.
explanations.B: A list command does not update scopes.
explanations.C: Listing definitions is inspection.
explanations.D: Resource governance inspection does not create users.

stem: An existing resource is noncompliant with a newly assigned policy. Which statement is appropriate?

choices.A: Evaluation identifies the issue; remediation depends on the effect and configuration
choices.B: The resource necessarily moves to another region
choices.C: Every effect instantly fixes every property
choices.D: The resource's Owner automatically becomes a guest

explanations.A: Not every effect repairs existing resources automatically.
explanations.B: Policy assignment does not imply migration.
explanations.C: Effects have different behavior.
explanations.D: Policy does not convert identity types.

stem: Why parameterize an allowed-locations policy definition?

choices.A: Every parameter creates a paid VM
choices.B: The definition becomes an authentication token
choices.D: One reusable rule can be assigned with different approved values

explanations.A: Parameters are not VM deployments.
explanations.B: Parameters do not create identity credentials.
explanations.C: They supply values rather than bypass governance.
explanations.D: Parameters adapt the rule to a scope's requirements.

stem: Which distinction correctly separates Policy from Azure RBAC?

choices.A: They are two names for the same assignment
choices.B: RBAC is only for storage tiers; Policy is only for guests
choices.C: Policy grants Owner; RBAC calculates costs
choices.D: RBAC grants permitted actions; Policy applies governance conditions

explanations.A: Role and policy assignments are different objects.
explanations.B: Both have broader management roles.
explanations.C: Those functions are reversed or unrelated.
explanations.D: They address complementary parts of resource access and compliance.

stem: Why might compliance results take time to reflect a change?

choices.A: Only newly created resources can ever be evaluated
choices.B: Every policy effect disables itself after a deployment
choices.C: Owner assignments bypass all compliance evaluation
choices.D: Policy evaluation and reporting have their own processing cycles

explanations.A: Existing resources can also be evaluated against assigned policies.
explanations.B: Effects do not generally turn off after one deployment.
explanations.C: Ownership does not universally remove Policy governance.
explanations.D: A recent change may not be reflected immediately.

stem: Which evidence helps troubleshoot a denied deployment?

choices.A: Only a resource-group delete lock
choices.B: Only the chosen VM SKU's estimated price
choices.C: The policy assignment and rule identified in the error
choices.D: Only the caller's role definition

explanations.A: A deployment policy error is not explained solely by a delete restriction.
explanations.B: The estimate does not identify the rule that rejected deployment.
explanations.C: That explains the governance condition the request violated.
explanations.D: Permission inspection may be useful, but the denial's policy details identify this governance rule.

stem: In this lab, how is Azure Policy explored?

choices.A: Remove all existing subscription assignments
choices.B: Create a new production initiative automatically
choices.C: Inspect built-in definitions without assigning them
choices.D: Apply a deny policy to every management group

explanations.A: That alters organizational governance.
explanations.B: The exercise is read-only for Policy.
explanations.C: The learner observes governance logic without imposing new rules.
explanations.D: That exceeds the lab's scope.

stem: Which lock permits authorized changes while preventing deletion?

choices.A: Reader
choices.B: CanNotDelete
choices.D: ReadOnly

explanations.A: Reader is a role rather than a lock.
explanations.B: It blocks deletion while allowing other permitted management changes.
explanations.C: Deny is a Policy effect rather than this lock level.
explanations.D: ReadOnly also blocks management updates.

stem: Which lock restricts management updates as well as deletion?

choices.A: Contributor
choices.B: Audit
choices.D: ReadOnly

explanations.A: That is a role granting management permissions.
explanations.B: That is a Policy effect reporting noncompliance.
explanations.C: That lock permits updates.
explanations.D: It restricts control-plane modification and deletion.

stem: A resource group has a CanNotDelete lock. What should happen to an authorized request to delete a child resource?

choices.A: The request always bypasses locks for Owners
choices.B: The inherited lock can block deletion
choices.C: The child ignores all parent locks
choices.D: The child becomes an Entra tenant

explanations.A: Owners must remove applicable locks first if authorized.
explanations.B: Parent locks apply to child resources.
explanations.C: Locks inherit through resource scope.
explanations.D: Locking does not change its resource type.

stem: Why should resource locks not be treated as blob-data backups?

choices.A: Locks encrypt every application response
choices.B: Locks replicate all data to three regions
choices.C: Locks protect management operations, not general data-plane content deletion
choices.D: Locks retain every deleted blob indefinitely

explanations.A: They are not a transport-encryption control.
explanations.B: They do not define replication.
explanations.C: Stored content needs suitable data protection.
explanations.D: They do not supply universal blob version retention.

stem: An Owner cannot delete a locked resource group. What explains this?

choices.A: The resource group must be in a sovereign cloud
choices.B: Applicable locks restrict operations across user roles
choices.D: The resource group's tags grant Reader

explanations.A: Locks are not limited to sovereign clouds.
explanations.B: Resource ownership does not bypass an existing lock automatically.
explanations.C: Owner normally has broad permissions.
explanations.D: Tags do not assign roles.

stem: What is required before deleting a resource protected by a lab-owned lock?

choices.A: Redeploy the resource's Bicep template unchanged
choices.B: Remove the relevant lock with appropriate permission
choices.D: Assign the caller another Reader role

explanations.A: Deployment does not automatically remove an applicable lock.
explanations.B: The lock must be removed before the protected delete operation.
explanations.C: Cost metadata does not remove the lock.
explanations.D: Reader does not remove the protected operation restriction.

stem: A resource group is unlocked, but one child has a delete lock. What can happen when deleting the group?

choices.A: The group deletion is blocked by the child lock
choices.B: Every unlocked child must be deleted first automatically
choices.C: The child lock grants Owner to the caller
choices.D: The child resource moves itself elsewhere

explanations.A: A locked child can prevent the group-wide operation.
explanations.B: The protected group deletion is blocked rather than assumed partial.
explanations.C: Locks do not grant permissions.
explanations.D: Locks do not relocate resources.

stem: Why should a team avoid adding a ReadOnly lock without understanding operational effects?

choices.A: Some routine control-plane operations require write or POST actions
choices.B: The lock resets every user's MFA
choices.D: The lock automatically deletes the VM disks

explanations.A: The lock can block operations that appear observational or operational.
explanations.B: It is not an authentication setting.
explanations.C: They do not prevent or perform cancellation.
explanations.D: It prevents changes rather than deleting disks.

stem: What distinguishes a resource lock from a Reader role assignment?

choices.A: A lock creates a new security principal
choices.B: Both are identical authentication-factor types
choices.C: Reader prevents data-plane deletion by every identity
choices.D: A lock restricts protected operations for applicable users; Reader grants one principal read access

explanations.A: A lock does not create an identity.
explanations.B: Neither is an authentication factor.
explanations.C: That overstates one role assignment.
explanations.D: They act at different control layers.

stem: Which permission issue can block creating or removing the lab's lock?

choices.A: The caller lacks blob-data Reader access
choices.B: The caller lacks Microsoft.Authorization/locks actions
choices.C: The caller lacks the VM login role
choices.D: The caller lacks permission to purchase reservations

explanations.A: Blob data access does not supply management-lock permissions.
explanations.B: Lock management needs appropriate explicit permissions.
explanations.C: Guest-OS login rights do not manage resource locks.
explanations.D: Billing commitments are unrelated to this lock-management action.

stem: A learner finds an inherited lock owned by another team. What should the lab cleanup do?

choices.A: Change the ownership tags to bypass checks
choices.B: Delete every inherited lock
choices.D: Stop and report the blocker without removing that lock

explanations.A: Ownership mismatch should remain a refusal.
explanations.B: That changes other teams' protections.
explanations.C: That is far beyond lab cleanup.
explanations.D: Unrelated governance controls must not be taken over.

stem: What does the lab lock named az900-protection demonstrate?

choices.A: Protection against accidental resource-group deletion
choices.B: Automatic data encryption for every file
choices.D: A billing limit that stops usage

explanations.A: The CanNotDelete lock is deliberately scoped to the owned lab group.
explanations.B: Locks do not encrypt file data.
explanations.C: Locks do not prevent datacenter failures.
explanations.D: Locks are not spending limits.

stem: Can a resource lock itself grant permission to update a resource?

choices.A: No; the user still needs suitable authorization
choices.B: Yes; removing a lock automatically grants Contributor
choices.C: Yes; ReadOnly assigns the Reader role to every identity
choices.D: Yes; CanNotDelete grants resource-write permission at its scope

explanations.A: A lock restricts permitted actions rather than granting them.
explanations.B: Removing a restriction does not add an authorization grant.
explanations.C: A restriction is not a role assignment.
explanations.D: The lock allows already-authorized changes but supplies no new grant.

stem: If a ReadOnly lock and a CanNotDelete lock both apply, which restriction is relevant?

choices.A: The user can choose which lock to honor
choices.B: The most recently named resource ignores both
choices.D: The cheaper resource's lock wins

explanations.A: The caller cannot select around the effective restriction.
explanations.B: Resource naming does not bypass inherited locks.
explanations.C: ReadOnly imposes stronger management restrictions.
explanations.D: Prices do not determine lock precedence.

stem: What should cleanup verify after removing its own lock and deleting its owned group?

choices.A: That all tenant users have been removed
choices.B: That Azure accepted the deletion request, without checking final existence
choices.C: That the resource group no longer exists
choices.D: That every subscription is empty

explanations.A: Identity deletion is outside the lab.
explanations.B: Request acceptance alone does not prove that asynchronous deletion finished successfully.
explanations.C: A requested deletion should be followed by absence verification.
explanations.D: Cleanup is limited to the lab's owned group.
